docs.title: 7.1 The OSI Reference Model (7 Layers)
docs.text: Developed by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO). [Faculty + General — Slide 32-35]

docs.title: ISO OSI Principles for Layering:
docs.text:
1. A layer should be created where a different abstraction is needed.
  2. Each layer should perform a well-defined function.
  3. The function of each layer should be chosen with an eye toward defining internationally standardized protocols.
  4. Layer boundaries should be chosen to minimize information flow across interfaces. [General — Slide 33]
+-----------------------------------+
| 7. Application Layer              |
+-----------------------------------+
| 6. Presentation Layer             |
+-----------------------------------+
| 5. Session Layer                  |
+-----------------------------------+
| 4. Transport Layer                |  <-- End-to-End Control
+-----------------------------------+
| 3. Network Layer                  |  <-- Subnet Routing
+-----------------------------------+
| 2. Data Link Layer                |  <-- Node-to-Node Hop
+-----------------------------------+
| 1. Physical Layer                 |  <-- Bit Stream Transmission
+-----------------------------------+

docs.title: Functions of the 7 OSI Layers:
docs.text:
1. Physical Layer (Layer 1): Transmits raw bits over a communication channel. Defines voltage levels, bit timing, pin counts, and transmission media specs. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  2. Data Link Layer (Layer 2): Takes raw transmission facility and transforms it into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors. Groups bits into frames, handles frame synchronization, error detection/correction, and flow control. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  3. Network Layer (Layer 3): Controls the operation of the subnet. Handles packet routing, congestion control, and internetworking between heterogeneous networks. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  4. Transport Layer (Layer 4): Accepts data from Session layer, splits it up into smaller units, passes these to Network layer, and ensures that all pieces arrive correctly at the other end. True end-to-end layer. [Faculty — Slide 35]
  5. Session Layer (Layer 5): Allows users on different machines to establish sessions between them. Provides dialog control (keeping track of whose turn it is to transmit) and synchronization (inserting checkpoints into long transfers). [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]
  6. Presentation Layer (Layer 6): Concerned with the syntax and semantics of the information transmitted. Handles data format conversions, encoding, data compression, and encryption. [Faculty — Slide 35 / General — Slide 57]
  7. Application Layer (Layer 7): Contains a variety of protocols that users commonly need (HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [Faculty — Slide 35] ──────

docs.title: Functions of the TCP/IP Layers:
docs.text:
1. Link Layer (Host-to-Network): Describes what links (such as serial lines or Ethernet) must do to meet the needs of the connectionless Internet layer. It is not really a layer in the strict sense, but an interface between hosts and transmission links. [General — Slide 36]
  2. Internet Layer: The linchpin of the architecture. Defines an official packet format and protocol called IP (Internet Protocol). Routes IP packets to their destinations independently. Handles packet delivery across network boundaries. [General — Slide 36]
  3. Transport Layer: Allows peer entities on the source and destination hosts to carry on a conversation. • TCP (Transmission Control Protocol): Reliable connection-oriented, byte-stream protocol. Provides flow control and congestion control. • UDP (User Datagram Protocol): Unreliable connectionless datagram protocol for applications that prefer low latency over reliability. [General — Slide 36]
  4. Application Layer: Contains all higher-level protocols (HTTP, Telnet, FTP, SMTP, DNS). [General — Slide 36] ──────

docs.title: A. Critique of the OSI Model ("The Four Bads") [Faculty + General — Slide 41]
docs.text:
1. Bad Timing: The OSI standards were published after TCP/IP was already heavily deployed in universities and industry ( The "Elephant Problem": TCP/IP took over the market before OSI was finalized).
  2. Bad Technology: Session and Presentation layers are virtually empty; Data Link and Physical layers are heavily redundant; complex and inefficient implementation.
  3. Bad Implementation: Initial OSI implementations were slow, bulky, and buggy compared to TCP/IP.
  4. Bad Politics: OSI was seen as government/telecom bureaucrat-driven, while TCP/IP was seen as open-source academic hacker- driven.

docs.title: B. Critique of the TCP/IP Model
docs.text:
1. Does not clearly distinguish between concepts of service, interface, and protocol.
  2. Not general; hard to adapt to describe protocol stacks other than TCP/IP.
  3. The Link layer is not really a layer in the architectural sense, but an interface.
  4. Completely omits physical and data link layer specifications. [General — Slide 41] ──────

docs.title: 8.1 ARPANET History & Paul Baran's Innovation
docs.text:
• In the 1960s, the US Defense Department wanted a command-and-control network that could survive a nuclear strike. • Centralized / Hierarchical Networks (Telephone System): Vulnerable because destruction of a single central switch breaks communication for all connected nodes. • Paul Baran's Distributed Packet Switching: Proposed a mesh network of interconnected switching nodes (IMPs - Interface Message Processors). Packets dynamically route around destroyed nodes. [Faculty — Slide 42-43 / General — Slide 43-46]

   (a) Centralized                    (b) Distributed Mesh (Baran)
       [Switch]                             (O)-----(O)-----(O)
      /   |    \                            | \     / |     / |
   (O)   (O)   (O)                          |  (O)----(O)---- |
                                            (O)------------- (O)

[Diagram: Centralized Telephone System vs Baran's Distributed Network — General Slide 43] ──────

docs.title: 8.3 Wireless LANs (IEEE 802.11)
docs.text:
• Infrastructure Mode: Wireless hosts connect to a wired network via a central Access Point ( AP). [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 49] • Ad-hoc Mode: Computers connect directly peer-to-peer without an AP. [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 49] • Wireless Transmission Challenges: • Multipath Fading: Signals reflect off walls/obstacles, arriving at the receiver out of phase and causing signal cancellation. [Faculty — Slide 47 / General — Slide 50] • Hidden Terminal Problem: Transmitters out of radio range of each other cause collisions at an intermediate receiver. [General — Slide 51]

──────

docs.text:
1. ITU-T (International Telecommunication Union - Telecommunication Standardization Sector): UN specialized agency for telecommunications standards. [Faculty — Slide 50]
  2. IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers): Develops local and metropolitan area network standards ( IEEE 802 committee). [Faculty — Slide 50]
  3. IETF (Internet Engineering Task Force): Publishes RFCs (Requests for Comments) defining Internet protocols (IP, TCP, HTTP). [Faculty — Slide 50]
  4. ISO (International Organization for Standardization): Formulated the OSI model. [Faculty — Slide 50] ──────

docs.title: 10.1 Speed & Bandwidth Prefixes (Base 10)
docs.text:
In networking communications, speed, data rate, and bandwidth use Powers of 10 (10³):

\[ 1 \text{ Kbps} = 10^3 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000 \text{ bps} \] \[ 1 \text{ Mbps} = 10^6 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000,000 \text{ bps} \] \[ 1 \text{ Gbps} = 10^9 \text{ bits/sec} = 1,000,000,000 \text{ bps} \]

[Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 55]

docs.title: 10.2 Storage & Memory Prefixes (Base 2)
docs.text:
Data storage (RAM, Disk sizes) uses Powers of 2 (2¹⁰):

\[ 1 \text{ KB} = 2^{10} \text{ bytes} = 1,024 \text{ bytes} \] \[ 1 \text{ MB} = 2^{20} \text{ bytes} = 1,048,576 \text{ bytes} \] \[ 1 \text{ GB} = 2^{30} \text{ bytes} = 1,073,741,824 \text{ bytes} \]

\[ 1 \text{ millisecond (ms)} = 10^{-3} \text{ seconds} \] \[ 1 \text{ microsecond (\mu s)} = 10^{-6} \text{ seconds} \] \[ 1 \text{ nanosecond (ns)} = 10^{-9} \text{ seconds} \]

docs.title: 11.1 Complete Formula Sheet
docs.text:
1. Network Metric Conversion (Bandwidth vs Storage): • Transmission Speed: 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits/sec • Memory Storage: 1 MB = 2²⁰ bytes = 1,048,576 bytes

docs.title: 11.2 Important Definitions
docs.text: • Computer Network: A collection of autonomous computers interconnected by communication links to exchange information. • Protocol: Rules governing the format and meaning of messages exchanged between peer entities at the same layer. • Service: Operations a lower layer provides to the layer directly above it via an interface. • Encapsulation: Adding layer headers/trailers to higher-layer SDUs as data moves down the stack. • Network Neutrality: Treating all Internet data traffic equally without discrimination by source, content, or application. ──────

docs.title: 11.3 Important Comparisons
docs.text: • Computer Network vs Distributed System: Explicit node visibility vs transparent unified system. • OSI vs TCP/IP: 7 layers vs 4 layers; theory-driven vs practical-driven; strict service/protocol separation vs merged concept. • Connection-Oriented vs Connectionless: Dedicated setup phase / in-order delivery vs independent datagram routing / possible reordering. ──────

docs.title: 11.4 Exam Revision Notes
docs.text: • Must-Know Diagrams: OSI 7-layer model, TCP/IP 4-layer model, Client-Server architecture, Encapsulation flow down stack. • Must-Know Concepts: Distinction between Service (vertical interface) and Protocol (horizontal peer rule). • Commonly Confused Prefixes: 1 Mbps in transmission bandwidth is 10⁶ bits/s, NOT 2²⁰. ──────────── Chapter 3 — Data Link Layer ──────

docs.title: 1.1 Role and Core Objectives of Data Link Layer
docs.text: • The Physical Layer delivers raw bits over a physical medium. However, physical channels suffer from: • Limited bandwidth • Signal distortions and bit errors • Propagation delays [Faculty — Slide 3] • Primary Objective of Data Link Layer: To transform a raw transmission facility into a line that appears free of undetected transmission errors to the Network Layer above it. [Faculty — Slide 4] ──────

docs.title: 1.2 Functions of Data Link Layer
docs.text:
1. Providing a well-defined service interface to the Network Layer.
  2. Framing: Grouping physical bit streams into discrete units called frames.
  3. Error Handling: Detecting and correcting errors (corrupted, lost, or duplicate frames).
  4. Flow Control: Regulating data transmission rate so fast senders do not overwhelm slow receivers. [Faculty — Slide 4] ──────

docs.title: 1.3 Layer Relationship & Implementation Architecture
docs.text:
• Virtual vs. Actual Communication: The Data Link Layer entities communicate virtually via a Data Link Protocol, but actual data flows down to the Physical Layer, across the physical medium, and back up. [Faculty — Slide 6 / General — Slide 9]

  Host A (Network Layer)                           Host B (Network Layer)
            |                                                ^
            v Virtual Data Link Protocol Path                |
  Host A (Data Link Layer) =====================> Host B (Data Link Layer)
            |                                                ^
            v Actual Physical Transmission Path              |
  Host A (Physical Layer)  ---------------------> Host B (Physical Layer)

• Hardware vs. Software Implementation: • NIC (Network Interface Card): Handles Physical Layer processes and time-critical Data Link Layer functions (framing, CRC hardware check, bit stuffing). • OS Kernel Device Driver: Handles higher link-layer logic, software timers, and Network Layer interactions on the main CPU. [Faculty — Slide 34 / General — Slide 32]

──────

docs.title: 1.4 Services Offered to Network Layer
docs.text:
1. Unacknowledged Connectionless Service: • Source sends independent frames without destination acknowledging them. • No connection setup or release. • Lost frames are not recovered by the link layer. • Use Cases: Low error rate channels (copper LANs) or real-time voice traffic where delay is worse than lost frames. [Faculty — Slide 8 / General — Slide 11]
  2. Acknowledged Connectionless Service: • Source sends independent frames, but each frame is individually acknowledged by the receiver. • If a frame does not arrive within a timeout period, it is retransmitted. • Use Cases: Highly unreliable wireless links (e.g., IEEE 802.11 Wi-Fi). [Faculty — Slide 9 / General — Slide 12]
  3. Acknowledged Connection-Oriented Service: • Connection is established before any data is sent. • Frames are numbered, acknowledged, and guaranteed to arrive exactly once and in the correct order. • Three Phases: Connection Establishment → Data Transfer → Connection Release. • Use Cases: Long-distance point-to-point satellite channels. [Faculty — Slide 10 / General — Slide 13]

──────

docs.title: 2.1 Why Framing is Necessary
docs.text: Physical Layer delivers a continuous stream of raw bits. To detect and recover from errors, the stream must be broken down into discrete Frames, so checksums can be computed for each frame. [Faculty — Slide 11 / General — Slide 14] ──────

docs.title: Method 1: Character Count / Byte Count
docs.text:
• Uses a field in the frame header to specify the total number of characters/bytes in the frame. • Mechanism: Receiver reads the count field to know where the frame ends. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 15]

  Frame 1 (5 bytes)     Frame 2 (5 bytes)     Frame 3 (8 bytes)
  +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+
  | 5 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | | 5 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | | 8 | 9 | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
  +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+ +---+---+---+---+---+---+---+---+

• Fatal Flaw / Disadvantage: If a single bit error corrupts the count field (e.g., a 5 becomes a 7), the receiver loses frame synchronization completely and cannot locate the start of subsequent frames. [Faculty — Slide 12 / General — Slide 16] ──────

docs.title: Method 2: Flag Bytes with Byte Stuffing (Character Stuffing)
docs.text:
• Delimits frames with special control bytes called FLAG bytes (e.g., ASCII DLE STX / DLE ETX or 0x7E). • Problem: What if the binary payload data itself contains the byte value matching FLAG? • Byte Stuffing Rule: • Sender inserts a special Escape byte (ESC) (e.g., 0x7D) immediately before any instance of FLAG or ESC occurring within the payload. • Receiver strips off the ESC byte upon reception. [Faculty — Slide 13-16 / General — Slide 17-19]

  Original Payload:       [ A ] [ FLAG ] [ B ]
  Transmitted (Stuffed):  [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ FLAG ] [ B ] [ FLAG ]

  Original Payload:       [ A ] [ ESC ] [ B ]
  Transmitted (Stuffed):  [ FLAG ] [ A ] [ ESC ] [ ESC ] [ B ] [ FLAG ]
──────

docs.title: Method 3: Flag Bits with Bit Stuffing
docs.text:
• Allows frames to contain an arbitrary number of bits (bit-oriented framing). • Frame start and end are marked by the special flag bit pattern: 01111110 (six consecutive 1s). • Bit Stuffing Rule (Sender): • Whenever sender's data link layer encounters FIVE consecutive 1s in the payload, it automatically stuffs a 0 bit immediately after them into the outgoing bit stream. • Destuffing Rule (Receiver): • When receiver sees five consecutive 1s followed by a 0 bit, it automatically strips out the 0 bit. • If followed by a 1 bit and a 0 bit, it is a valid end-of-frame FLAG (01111110). • If followed by two 1 bits, an error has occurred (01111111). [Faculty — Slide 17-20 / General — Slide 20-22]

  Original Data:      01101111111001111101
  Stuffed Stream:     0110111110110011111001
                              ^         ^
                        (Stuffed 0s inserted)
──────

docs.title: Method 4: Physical Layer Coding Violations
docs.text: • Used in networks where Physical Layer encoding has inherent redundancy (e.g., Manchester encoding where every bit period has a signal transition). • High-High or Low-Low signals are invalid data transitions; they are used as delimiters to mark frame boundaries. [Faculty — Slide 21 / General — Slide 24] ──────

docs.title: 3.1 Error Types
docs.text: • Single-Bit Error: Only 1 bit of a data unit is inverted. • Burst Error: 2 or more bits in a data unit are corrupted. Length of burst k is measured from the first corrupted bit to the last corrupted bit. [Faculty — Slide 22] ──────

docs.title: 3.2 Error Control Strategies
docs.text: • Forward Error Correction (FEC): Sender includes enough redundant bits for receiver to detect AND correct errors without retransmission. Used on noisy/high-delay channels (wireless, satellite). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25] • Automatic Repeat reQuest (ARQ): Sender includes just enough redundancy to detect errors. Receiver requests retransmission upon detecting error. Used on low-noise channels (optical fiber). [Faculty — Slide 22 / General — Slide 25] ──────

docs.title: Definition: Hamming Distance
docs.text: The number of bit positions in which two binary codewords differ. Calculated by performing an XOR operation between two codewords and counting the number of 1s in the result. [Faculty — Slide 24 / General — Slide 26]

docs.title: Formula: Error Detection Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge d + 1 \]

To detect d single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) of the code must be at least d + 1. [Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: Formula: Error Correction Requirement
docs.text:
\[ d_{\text{min}} \ge 2p + 1 \]

To correct p single-bit errors, the minimum Hamming distance \(d_{\text{min}}\) must be at least 2p + 1. [Faculty — Slide 25]

docs.title: 3.4 The Hamming Code (Single-Bit Error Correcting Code)
Rules of Hamming Code Construction:
docs.text:
1. Bit positions are numbered starting at 1 (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7...).
  2. Check bits (Parity bits \(P_k\)) are placed at positions that are powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…(\(2^k\)).
  3. Data bits (\(D_j\)) fill all remaining positions (3, 5, 6, 7, 9…). [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: Formula: Relationship Between Data Bits and Redundant Check Bits
docs.text:
For m data bits and r redundant check bits:

\[ (m + r + 1) \le 2^r \]

[Faculty — Slide 27]

docs.title: Step-by-Step Worked Numerical Example 1: Hamming Code Encoding
docs.text:
Problem: Encode the 4-bit data message \(D = 1101_2\) (\(D_4=1,D_3=1,D_2=0,D_1=1\)) into a (7,4) Hamming code using EVEN parity.

  • Given: Data \(m = 4\) bits (1101). \(r = 3\) check bits are required because:
\[ (m+r+1) \le 2^r \] \[ (4+3+1) \le 2^3 \] \[ 8 \le 8 \]

docs.title: Bit Positioning:
docs.text:
Bit Position:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7
Bit Type:     P1  P2  D1  P4  D2  D3  D4
Bit Value:    ?   ?   1   ?   0   1   1

docs.title: Parity Computation Groups:
docs.text:
• \(P_1\) checks positions (1,3,5,7):
\[ P_1,D_1,D_2,D_4 = P_1,1,0,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_1 = 0 \]
  • \(P_2\) checks positions (2,3,6,7):
\[ P_2,D_1,D_3,D_4 = P_2,1,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_2 = 1 \]
  • \(P_4\) checks positions (4,5,6,7):
\[ P_4,D_2,D_3,D_4 = P_4,0,1,1 \]

For EVEN parity:

\[ P_4 = 0 \]

docs.title: Final Transmitted Codeword:
docs.text:
\[ \text{Codeword} = \mathbf{0110011} \]

[Faculty — Slide 29]

docs.title: 3.6 Internet Checksum (UDP Worked Numerical Example) [Faculty — Slide 33]
docs.text: • Data is treated as a sequence of 16-bit integers. • Integers are added together using 1's complement arithmetic. • The final sum is bitwise inverted (NOT operation).

docs.title: 4.1 Definition
docs.text: Mechanisms to prevent a fast transmitting node from swamping a slower receiving node with more data than its buffers can store. [Faculty — Slide 27 / General — Slide 27]

docs.title: 4.2 Three Flow Control Strategies
docs.text:
Flow Control Strategies
                                   |
         +-------------------------+-------------------------+
         |                         |                         |
   Feedback-Based             Rate-Based               Credit-Based
 (Receiver sends ACKs)    (Built-in Rate Limit)   (Receiver grants credits)
  1. Feedback-Based Flow Control: Receiver sends feedback messages back to the sender giving explicit permission to transmit more data (e.g., Stop-and-Wait, Sliding Window ACKs). [Faculty — Slide 28 / General — Slide 28]
  2. Rate-Based Flow Control: Protocol mechanism limits transmission to a fixed data rate built-in, without explicit feedback frames. [Faculty — Slide 29 / General — Slide 29]
  3. Credit-Based Flow Control: Receiver grants sender explicit window credits (in bytes or frames). Sender deducts credits for each byte sent and stops when credits reach zero. [Faculty — Slide 30 / General — Slide 30] ──────

docs.title: 5.1 Protocol Environment Architecture
docs.text:
In Tanenbaum framework, protocol code interacts with lower (Physical) and upper (Network) layers via interface primitives:

• to_network_layer(p) / from_network_layer(&p) • to_physical_layer(&f) / from_physical_layer(&f) • start_timer(k) / stop_timer(k) • wait_for_event(&event) [Faculty — Slide 35-36 / General — Slide 34-36] ──────

docs.title: Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is strictly unidirectional (Simplex).
  2. Physical channel is completely error-free.
  3. Receiver's network layer has infinite processing speed and buffer space (No flow control needed). [Faculty — Slide 37 / General — Slide 37]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender loops infinitely fetching packets from network layer and sending frames. Receiver loops infinitely waiting for frames and handing packets up.

// Sender (Utopian)
void sender1(void) {
    frame s; packet buffer;
    while (true) {
        from_network_layer(&buffer);
        s.info = buffer;
        to_physical_layer(&s);
    }
}
──────

docs.title: 5.3 Protocol 2: Simplex Stop-and-Wait Protocol for Error-Free Channel
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Communication is unidirectional.
  2. Physical channel is error-free.
  3. Receiver has finite buffer capacity and limited processing speed. [Faculty — Slide 39 / General — Slide 39]

docs.title: Mechanism:
docs.text:
Sender sends 1 frame, then stops and waits until receiver sends back an explicit ACK dummy frame signaling it is ready for the next frame.

     Sender Machine                                Receiver Machine
  +------------------+                          +-------------------+
  | Send Frame 0     | -----------------------> | Receive Frame 0   |
  | (Wait for ACK)   |                          | Pass to Network L |
  |                  | <----------------------- | Send Dummy ACK    |
  | Receive ACK      |                          | (Wait for Frame)  |
  | Send Frame 1     | -----------------------> |                   |
  +------------------+                          +-------------------+
──────

docs.title: 5.4 Protocol 3: Simplex Stop-and-Wait for Noisy Channel (PAR)
Key Assumptions:
docs.text:
1. Channel is noisy: frames can be corrupted or lost completely.
  2. ACKs can also be corrupted or lost. [Faculty — Slide 42 / General — Slide 42]

docs.title: Key Mechanisms added:
docs.text:
1. Timer & Retransmission: Sender sets a timer upon transmitting a frame. If ACK does not arrive before timer expires, sender retransmits.
  2. 1-Bit Sequence Numbers (0 and 1): Prevents duplicate frame acceptance when an ACK is delayed/lost. [Faculty — Slide 44 / General — Slide 44]

Normal Sequence: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver --(ACK 0)--> Sender --(Frame 1)--> Receiver

Lost ACK Scenario: Sender --(Frame 0)--> Receiver (Gets Frame 0, Sends ACK 0 [LOST!]) Sender Timer Expires! Sender --(Retransmit Frame 0)--> Receiver (Sees Seq 0 duplicate, discards payload, re-sends ACK 0!) ──────

docs.title: 6.1 Bidirectional Transmission & Piggybacking
docs.text: • Piggybacking: Temporarily delaying an outgoing ACK so it can be hooked onto the header of the next outgoing data frame. • Timer for Piggybacking: If no outgoing data frame is generated within a short timeout, a separate ACK frame must be sent to avoid sender timeout. [Faculty — Slide 48 / General — Slide 48] ──────

docs.title: 6.2 Sequence Number Space & Window Concept
docs.text: • Sequence numbers range from 0 to MAX_SEQ = 2ⁿ - 1 (for n-bit sequence numbers). • Sender Window (Wₛ): Contains sequence numbers of frames sent but not yet acknowledged. • Receiver Window (Wᵣ): Contains sequence numbers of frames receiver is willing to accept. [Faculty — Slide 49 / General — Slide 49] ──────

docs.title: 6.3 Protocol 4: One-Bit Sliding Window (Wₛ = 1,Wᵣ = 1)
docs.text: • Stop-and-Wait protocol implemented using a 1-bit sequence number (0 or 1). • Simultaneous Start Anomaly: If both sender and receiver initiate transmission at the exact same moment, duplicate frames are transmitted back and forth, wasting half the link bandwidth. [Faculty — Slide 52 / General — Slide 52] ──────

docs.title: Formula: Frame Transmission Time
docs.text:
[ T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{L}{B} ]

• L = Frame length in bits. • B = Link bandwidth in bits per second (bps).

docs.title: Formula: Round-Trip Time (RTT)
docs.text:
[ \text{RTT} = 2 \cdot T_{\text{prop}} ]

*

T prop

= One-way propagation delay over link.

docs.title: Formula: Stop-and-Wait Efficiency (η)
docs.text:
[ \eta = \frac{T_{\text{frame}}}{T_{\text{frame}} + \text{RTT}} = \frac{1}{1 + 2a} ] where

    T

a = ──────

docs.title: Step-by-Step Worked Numerical Example 4: Satellite Channel Efficiency [Faculty — Slide 50 / General — Slide 53-54]
Problem
docs.text: • Bandwidth B = 50 kbps = 50,000 bps • Round-Trip Delay RTT = 500 ms = 0.5 seconds • Frame Size L = 1000 bits • Calculate the link efficiency under Stop-and-Wait (Window = 1), and find the minimum window size W needed for 100% utilization.

docs.title: Step 1: Calculate Frame Transmission Time (
docs.text:
T
 frame

) [ T_{\text{frame}} = \frac{1000 \text{ bits}}{50,000 \text{ bps}} = 0.020 \text{ seconds} = 20 \text{ ms} ]

docs.title: Step 2: Calculate Total Cycle Time (
docs.text:
T

) [ T_{\text{total}} = T_{\text{frame}} + \text{RTT} = 20 \text{ ms} + 500 \text{ ms} = 520 \text{ ms} ]

docs.title: Step 3: Calculate Channel Efficiency (η)
docs.text: [ \eta = \frac{T_{\text{frame}}}{T_{\text{total}}} = \frac{20 \text{ ms}}{520 \text{ ms}} \approx 0.03846 = \mathbf{3.85\%} ] (The link is idle 96.15% of the time!)

docs.title: Step 4: Calculate Window Size (W) needed for 100% Efficiency
docs.text: [ W \ge \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{T_{\text{frame}}} = \frac{520 \text{ ms}}{20 \text{ ms}} = \mathbf{26 \text{ frames}} \quad (\text{or } 1 + 2a = 1 + 2(12.5) = 26) ] ──────

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text: • Sender Window Wₛ > 1, Receiver Window Wᵣ = 1. • Receiver discards all out-of-order frames and sends cumulative ACKs for the last correctly received in-order frame. • On timeout, sender retransmits ALL unacknowledged outstanding frames starting from the oldest unacked frame. [Faculty — Slide 51 / General — Slide 56]

docs.title: Crucial Rule: Maximum Window Size for Go-Back-N
Formula: Maximum Sender Window Size (GBN)
docs.text:
[ W_s \le \text{MAX_SEQ} = 2^n - 1 ]

• Reason / Proof: If sequence numbers are 3 bits (0 to 7, size 8), and Wₛ = 8: • Sender transmits frames 0..7. Receiver receives all 8 frames and expects frame 0 next. • All ACKs are lost in transit. • Sender timeout occurs and retransmits frame 0. • Receiver cannot distinguish whether frame 0 is a retransmission or a brand new frame 0 from the next sequence cycle! • Setting Wₛ = 7 (2ⁿ - 1) prevents this ambiguity. [Faculty — Slide 52 / General — Slide 58]

──────

docs.title: Key Characteristics:
docs.text: • Sender Window Wₛ > 1, Receiver Window Wᵣ > 1. • Receiver accepts and buffers out-of-order frames within its window. • Receiver sends a NAK (Negative Acknowledgement) to trigger fast retransmission of only the missing frame. • Sender retransmits ONLY the single corrupted/missing frame upon receiving a NAK or timer expiry. [Faculty — Slide 57 / General — Slide 68]

docs.title: Crucial Rule: Maximum Window Size for Selective Repeat
Formula: Maximum Window Size (Selective Repeat)
docs.text:
[ W_s = W_r \le \frac{\text{MAX_SEQ} + 1}{2} = 2^{n-1} ]

• Reason / Proof: If sequence space is 0..7 (8 numbers), max window size is 4. • If Wₛ = 5, sender sends 0,1,2,3,4. Receiver receives and ACKs them, advancing its window to 5,6,7,0,1. • If all ACKs are lost, sender retransmits frame 0. • Receiver's new window contains 0; it would mistakenly accept the old duplicate frame 0 as new data! • Restricting Wₛ ≤ 2ⁿ⁻¹ guarantees no overlap between old and new sequence windows. [Faculty — Slide 58 / General — Slide 77]

──────

docs.title: 7.1 Packet over SONET (PoS)
docs.text: • Used over wide-area optical fiber backbone links. • Uses SONET (Synchronous Optical Network) at the Physical layer and PPP (Point-to-Point Protocol) at the Data Link layer. [Faculty — Slide 64 / General — Slide 80] ──────

docs.title: Three Core Components of PPP:
docs.text:
1. Framing Method: HDLC-based frame format with byte stuffing.
  2. LCP (Link Control Protocol): For bringing links up, testing them, negotiating options, and bringing them down cleanly.
  3. NCP (Network Control Protocol): Negotiates network-layer options (e.g., assigning IP addresses via IPCP). [Faculty — Slide 65 / General — Slide 81]

docs.text: \[ BDP=B \times RTT \]

docs.title: 8.2 Important Definitions
docs.text: • Framing: Grouping bits from the Physical Layer into discrete frames with headers/trailers. • Bit Stuffing: Inserting a 0 bit after five consecutive 1s to prevent payload data from matching the 01111110 flag. • Hamming Distance: Number of bit positions in which two binary codewords differ. • Piggybacking: Delaying ACKs to attach them to outgoing data frame headers. • Pipelining: Transmitting multiple frames before receiving an acknowledgment for the first frame. ──────

docs.title: 8.3 Important Comparisons
docs.text: • Forward Error Correction (FEC) vs ARQ: Self-correcting via redundancy (high overhead, noisy links) vs detecting & retransmitting (low overhead, clean links). • Byte Stuffing vs Bit Stuffing: ESC byte insertion before FLAG/ESC bytes vs single 0 bit insertion after five 1s. • Go-Back-N vs Selective Repeat: Receiver window 1 / discards out-of-order / retransmits whole window vs Receiver window > 1 / buffers out-of-order / retransmits only missing frame via NAK. ──────

docs.title: 8.4 Exam Revision Sheet
docs.text:
• Must-Know Numerical Calculations: 1. Hamming Code encoding and syndrome-based error location. 2. CRC polynomial long division (XOR) and remainder determination. 3. UDP Checksum 1's complement addition. 4. Channel efficiency (η) and required pipelining window size (W). • Must-Know Proof Rules: 1. Why Go-Back-N window cannot exceed 2ⁿ - 1. 2. Why Selective Repeat window cannot exceed 2ⁿ⁻¹. • Must-Know Diagram Structures: 1. Bit stuffing vs character stuffing frame formats. 2. Sliding window sender/receiver state diagrams. 3. PPP frame format and state transition diagram.

──────

docs.title: 2. Chapter Overview
docs.text:
This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of Data Analysis and Visualisation (DAV). It covers the definitions of data, the data lifecycle, types of data, quantitative vs qualitative analysis, and the end-to-end data analysis process. It explores Big Data (5 V's), the DIKW model, process models (CRISP-DM and KDD), analytics types (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive), visualization techniques, standard software tools/libraries, open data sources, and industry case studies.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slides 1-44; 1.Introduction to DAV.pdf]

docs.title: 3. Fundamental Concepts: The DIKW Hierarchy & Data Life Cycle
docs.text:
The DIKW Model describes the transformation of raw facts into strategic actions:

\[ \text{Data} \longrightarrow \text{Information} \longrightarrow \text{Knowledge} \longrightarrow \text{Wisdom} \] 
graph BT
    A["Data: Raw Facts"] --> B["Information: Contextualized Data"]
    B --> C["Knowledge: Actionable Information"]
    C --> D["Wisdom: Applied Knowledge"]

docs.title: Data Life Cycle
docs.text:
The data lifecycle represents the sequence of stages that data goes through from its initial generation to its final visualization and analysis. 

flowchart LR
    A[Generation/Collection] --> B[Storage]
    B --> C[Processing/Transformation]
    C --> D[Analysis]
    D --> E[Visualization/Communication]

[Source: 1.Introduction to DAV.pdf, Slide 15; ch1_text.txt, Slide 15]

docs.title: Definition: Data
docs.text: Meaning: Raw, unprocessed facts, figures, and symbols without context. Formal definition: Raw facts or figures without any context. It can be numbers, words, measurements, observations, or even just symbols. Intuition: Before processing, data is just raw material waiting to be evaluated. Example: Sensor readings: \(38, 39, 40\).

docs.title: Definition: Information
docs.text: Meaning: Data that is structured and given meaning. Formal definition: Data organized and structured to answer "who", "what", "where", and "when". Intuition: After analysis, data becomes information or knowledge because context is added. Example: The readings \(38^\circ\text{C}, 39^\circ\text{C}, 40^\circ\text{C}\) represent daily peak temperatures in July.

docs.title: Definition: Knowledge
docs.text: Meaning: The synthesis of information. Formal definition: Synthesized information revealing patterns and answering "how". Intuition: The ability to find actionable trends within the information. Example: Understanding that temperatures above \(35^\circ\text{C}\) trigger a \(40\%\) surge in air conditioner purchases.

docs.title: Definition: Wisdom
docs.text: Meaning: The application of knowledge. Formal definition: Evaluated knowledge incorporating judgment to answer "why" and guide strategy. Intuition: Making a strategic business decision based on the generated knowledge. Example: Pre-emptively increasing regional warehouse inventory of air conditioners in May.

docs.title: Definition: Data Analysis
docs.text: Meaning: Asking questions of the data to find actionable insights. Formal definition: The process of making sense of the data. Analysis means asking questions to the data and finding answers. Intuition: Extracting useful signals from collected records to aid decision-making. Example: For a small online shop, analyzing what products people bought, when they bought them, and how much they paid to determine if discounts should be offered on weekends.

docs.title: Definition: Data Visualisation
docs.text:
Meaning: Creating visual artifacts of data. Formal definition: Turning numbers into visuals, like graphs, charts, and dashboards, so people can understand the story behind the data quickly and easily. Intuition: Because human brains process images faster than raw text or tables, charts can show trends or problems at a glance without reading rows of numbers. Example: A pie chart showing how sales are split between regions, or a line graph showing revenue changes over time.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slides 14, 18, 24]

  3. Grouped (Class Table) Data: Aggregated observations into continuous class intervals with frequencies.
  4. Example:
Class Interval (CI) Class Midpoint (\(x_i\)) Frequency (\(f_i\)) Cumulative Frequency (\(CF\)) \(10 - 15\) \(12.5\) \(2\) \(2\) \(15 - 20\) \(17.5\) \(2\) \(4\) \(20 - 25\) \(22.5\) \(3\) \(7\) \(25 - 30\) \(27.5\) \(3\) \(10\) Total — \(N = \sum f_i = 10\) —

docs.title: 8. Data Transformation & Visualisation
docs.text: "Visualization provides a unique perspective on the dataset. Visualization is critical to data analysis. It provides a front line of attack, revealing intricate structure in data that cannot be absorbed in any other way. We discover unimagined effects, and we challenge imagined ones." — William S. Cleveland, Visualizing Data

docs.title: Data Transformation
docs.text:
Data transformation is the process of converting data or information from one format to another, usually from the format of a source system into the required format of a new destination system.

It can be divided into two steps: 1. Data mapping: Maps data elements from the source data system to the destination data system and captures any transformation that must occur. 2. Code generation: Creates the actual transformation program.

docs.title: How to Visualize Data
docs.text:
Depending on the goal, different visual components are used: - Tables: Very powerful when dealing with a relatively small number of data points. - Charts: Allow mapping dimensions in data to visual properties of geometric shapes (e.g., Bar charts, Pie charts). - Maps: The power of maps is to re-connect the data to our physical world. - Graphs: Used for showing inter-connections (edges) between data points (nodes).

docs.title: 10. Industry Applications & Case Studies
docs.text:
Data visualization and analysis assist almost every company or sector that aims to grow by giving them the vision to increase customer satisfaction.

Industry Use Case / Benefit Healthcare Hospitals use visualizations to track patient wait times and identify bottlenecks in the emergency department, allowing for better resource allocation. Marketing Marketers visualize data from social media and website analytics to analyze campaign performance, understand consumer behavior/preferences, and identify trends. Finance Professionals interpret complex financial data quickly. Investment firms use interactive charts to visualize stock prices or compare portfolios to spot anomalies impacting decisions. Manufacturing Empowers manufacturers to optimize operations by monitoring KPIs. Visual metrics on throughput or defect rates help identify inefficiencies promptly. Technology In cybersecurity, visualizations allow analysts to detect patterns in network traffic efficiently and respond swiftly to potential threats.

[Source: ch1_text.txt, Slide 31, 43]

docs.title: Formula:
docs.text: \[ \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \]

docs.title: Where:
docs.text:
• \(\bar{x}\) = Sample Mean
  • \(n\) = Total number of observations in the dataset
  • \(x_i\) = \(i\)-th individual observation

docs.title: Meaning:
docs.text: Computes the arithmetic average of a discrete set of unweighted, raw observations.

docs.title: 2. Data Aggregation Formula (Grouped Class Table Mean)
Formula:
docs.text: \[ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i x_i}{N} \quad \text{where } N = \sum_{i=1}^{k} f_i \]

docs.title: Where:
docs.text:
• \(\bar{x}\) = Estimated Mean for grouped data
  • \(k\) = Total number of class intervals
  • \(f_i\) = Frequency of the \(i\)-th class interval
  • \(x_i\) = Midpoint of the \(i\)-th class interval, calculated as \(\frac{\text{Lower Limit} + \text{Upper Limit}}{2}\)
  • \(N\) = Total frequency across all classes

docs.title: Meaning:
docs.text: Estimates the central location of grouped data when individual values are unknown, assuming observations are evenly distributed within each class interval.

docs.title: Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Data: Raw, unprocessed facts, figures, and symbols without context.
  • Information: Data organized and structured to answer who, what, where, and when.
  • Knowledge: Synthesized information revealing patterns and answering how.
  • Wisdom: Evaluated knowledge incorporating judgment to answer why and guide strategy.
  • Data Analysis: Process of making sense of data by asking questions and finding answers.
  • Data Visualisation: Turning numbers into visual representations to clearly communicate findings.
  • Descriptive Analytics: Summarizing historical observations (What happened?).
  • Diagnostic Analytics: Determining causes of past events (Why did it happen?).
  • Predictive Analytics: Forecasting future outcomes (What will happen?).
  • Prescriptive Analytics: Optimizing actions based on predictive outcomes (What should we do?).
  • CRISP-DM: Standardized 6-phase data mining lifecycle.
  • Data Transformation: Converting data from a source format to a required destination format via mapping and code generation.

docs.title: Key Questions & Model Answers
docs.text:
Q1: Contrast Descriptive Analytics and Prescriptive Analytics with examples. A: - Descriptive Analytics focuses on summarizing historical data to answer "What happened?". It uses summary statistics, aggregations, and standard reporting tools. Example: A retail store generating a report showing that total sales revenue last month was \(\$50,000\). - Prescriptive Analytics goes beyond prediction to suggest optimal courses of action to answer "What should we do?". It uses mathematical optimization, simulation, and decision rules. Example: An automated inventory system recommending the exact reorder quantity of 200 units for Product X now to maximize profit and prevent stockouts.

Q2: What is the difference between Quantitative and Qualitative data? Provide two examples of each. A: - Quantitative Data consists of numerical values that can be measured or counted objectively. - Examples: Student GPA (\(3.8\)), Monthly Income (\(\$4,500\)). - Qualitative Data consists of non-numerical categorical descriptions that classify attributes based on traits or qualities. - Examples: Customer Feedback ("Excellent"), T-shirt size ("Medium").

Q3: How does raw ungrouped data differ from grouped class table data? Given raw values \(\{12, 14, 15, 18, 22, 24\}\), calculate the mean using both raw form and a grouped frequency table with intervals \(10-20\) and \(20-30\). A: - Difference: Raw ungrouped data retains every single exact observation. Grouped class table data aggregates individual values into continuous range intervals with frequency counts \(f_i\), replacing individual points with class midpoints \(x_i\). - Calculation: 1. Ungrouped Mean:

\[ \bar{x} = \frac{12 + 14 + 15 + 18 + 22 + 24}{6} = \frac{105}{6} = 17.5 \]
  1. Grouped Class Table Mean:
    • Interval \(10-20\): Midpoint \(x_1 = 15\), Frequency \(f_1 = 4\) (values: \(12, 14, 15, 18\))
    • Interval \(20-30\): Midpoint \(x_2 = 25\), Frequency \(f_2 = 2\) (values: \(22, 24\))
\[ \bar{x}_{\text{grouped}} = \frac{(4 \times 15) + (2 \times 25)}{4 + 2} = \frac{60 + 50}{6} = \frac{110}{6} \approx 18.33 \]

Q4: List and briefly explain the 6 phases of the CRISP-DM model. A: 1. Business Understanding: Define project objectives and requirements from a business perspective. 2. Data Understanding: Collect, explore, and verify data quality to identify initial insights. 3. Data Preparation: Clean, construct, integrate, and format datasets for modeling. 4. Modeling: Select and apply various modeling techniques (e.g., regression, classification). 5. Evaluation: Thoroughly assess models to ensure they meet business goals. 6. Deployment: Integrate models into operational environments for ongoing decision-making.

Q5: Explain the two steps of Data Transformation. A: 1. Data mapping: The process of mapping data elements from the source schema to the target schema, defining rules for data transformation. 2. Code generation: Creating the executable transformation software program or query that carries out the defined mapping logic.

docs.title: Ch 2 - Types of Data
docs.text: Course: Data Analysis and Visualization Primary Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf Files Integrated: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Existing Notes

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text: This chapter explores the foundational concepts of data in Data Analysis and Visualization. It begins by defining data, data sources (primary and secondary), and the Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process. It then covers the fundamental classifications of data, distinguishing between qualitative and quantitative data, as well as discrete and continuous attributes. A deep dive into the four Stevens' levels of measurement (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio) provides the mathematical framework for understanding permissible operations on different data types. Data representation formats are discussed in detail, contrasting raw ungrouped data with grouped frequency distributions, including full calculations for class boundaries, midpoints, and cumulative frequencies. Finally, the chapter categorizes digital data into structured, semi-structured, and unstructured formats, examining their sources, handling techniques, and practical examples such as airport and shopping mall scenarios. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: Definition: Data
docs.text: Meaning: Data is a collection of facts, numbers, words, observations, or other useful information. Formal definition: Raw, unorganized facts that need to be processed; data can be something simple and seemingly random and useless until it is organized. Intuition: We live in the "data age" rather than just the "information age". Raw data points are transformed into valuable insights through processing and analysis, which improve decision-making and drive better business outcomes. Example: A list of temperatures recorded over a week: \(22^\circ\text{C}, 24^\circ\text{C}, 19^\circ\text{C}\). [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: Definition: Data Mining
docs.text: Meaning: The process of discovering interesting patterns and knowledge from large amounts of data. Formal definition: The application of specific algorithms for extracting patterns from data. Intuition: It is the analytical step of the "Knowledge Discovery in Databases" process, turning raw data into useful information. Example: Analyzing supermarket transaction data to find that customers who buy diapers also frequently buy beer. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: 3. Sources of Data
docs.text: Data can be broadly classified into two main sources based on its origin:

docs.title: 1. Primary Data Sources
docs.text: Data collected firsthand for a specific research purpose. - Door to Door Surveys: Directly asking individuals questions. - Student Thesis: Original research conducted by students. - Personal Interviews: One-on-one structured or unstructured conversations.

docs.title: 2. Secondary Data Sources
docs.text:
Data that has already been collected by someone else and is available for use. - Internet: Web scraping, open data portals. - Books: Published literature and datasets. - Newspaper: Historical records, articles, financial reports.

graph TD
    DS[Data Sources] --> PDS[Primary Data Sources]
    DS --> SDS[Secondary Data Sources]

    PDS --> D2D[Door to Door Surveys]
    PDS --> ST[Student Thesis]
    PDS --> PI[Personal Interviews]

    SDS --> Int[Internet]
    SDS --> Bks[Books]
    SDS --> News[Newspaper]
[Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 3]

docs.title: 4. Process of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD)
docs.text: The KDD process outlines how raw data is transformed into useful knowledge.

docs.title: Algorithm: KDD Process
docs.text:
Purpose: To systematically extract valuable knowledge from raw data. Procedure: 1. Data cleaning: Remove noise and inconsistencies from the data. 2. Data integration: Combine data from multiple heterogeneous sources. 3. Data selection: Retrieve the relevant data for analysis from the database. 4. Data transformation: Convert and summarize data into appropriate forms for mining. 5. Data mining: Apply intelligent methods and algorithms to extract patterns. 6. Pattern evaluation: Identify truly interesting and useful patterns representing knowledge. 7. Knowledge presentation: Use visualization and representation techniques to present the mined knowledge to users.

flowchart TD
    DB[(Databases/Flat files)] --> |Cleaning and integration| DW[(Data Warehouse)]
    DW --> |Selection and transformation| DM_Data[Data for mining]
    DM_Data --> |Data mining| Pat[Patterns]
    Pat --> |Evaluation and presentation| Know[Knowledge]
[Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 4]

docs.title: 5. Fundamental Data Classifications
docs.text:
graph TD
    Data[Data Classifications]
    Data --> Qual[Qualitative / Categorical]
    Data --> Quant[Quantitative / Numerical]

    Qual --> Nom[Nominal: Unordered]
    Qual --> Ord[Ordinal: Ordered]

    Quant --> Disc[Discrete: Countable]
    Quant --> Cont[Continuous: Measurable]

    Cont --> Int[Interval: Arbitrary Zero]
    Cont --> Rat[Ratio: True Zero]

docs.title: Definition: Qualitative Data
docs.text: Meaning: Non-numerical categorical data representing attributes, properties, or qualities. Formal definition: Data that describes categories or groups that cannot be mathematically quantified in a meaningful way. Intuition: Answers the question "What type?" or "Which category?". Example: Eye color (\(\text{Blue}, \text{Brown}, \text{Green}\)), Payment status (\(\text{Paid}, \text{Pending}\)).

docs.title: Definition: Quantitative Data
docs.text: Meaning: Numerical data representing measurable quantities on which arithmetic operations can be performed. Formal definition: Data expressing a certain quantity, amount, or range, represented by numbers. Intuition: Answers the question "How much?" or "How many?". Example: Height (\(175\text{ cm}\)), Temperature (\(25^\circ\text{C}\)), Account balance (\(\$1500\)).

docs.title: Definition: Discrete Data
docs.text: Meaning: Quantitative data taking on distinct, separated, and countable values. Formal definition: A variable \(X\) is discrete if its set of possible values is finite or countably infinite. Intuition: Values that can be counted using integers. There are no possible values between two adjacent discrete points. Example: Number of customer visits \(X \in \{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}\).

docs.title: Definition: Continuous Data
docs.text: Meaning: Quantitative data taking on any real numerical value within a given continuous interval. Formal definition: A variable \(X\) is continuous if it can take on any value in the set of real numbers \(\mathbb{R}\) over some interval. Intuition: Values that are measured. Between any two continuous data points, there are infinitely many other potential points. Example: Exact weight \(W \in (0, \infty)\text{ kg}\). [Source: Existing Notes]

docs.title: 6. Levels of Measurement (Stevens' Scales)
docs.text: Data is further refined into four hierarchical levels of measurement, proposed by Stanley Smith Stevens. Each level possesses distinct mathematical properties.

docs.title: 1. Nominal Scale
docs.text: Meaning: Categorical data consisting of discrete categories without any inherent order or ranking. Mathematical Property: Only equality checks are permissible. We can only determine if \(x_i = x_j\) or \(x_i \neq x_j\). Permissible Operations: Mode, Chi-Square tests. Intuition: Numbers act merely as labels or tags. Example: Gender (\(1=\text{Male}, 2=\text{Female}\)), Zip Codes (\(90210, 10001\)), Blood Type (\(A, B, AB, O\)).

docs.title: 2. Ordinal Scale
docs.text: Meaning: Categorical data where the categories have a meaningful rank or natural order, but the intervals between ranks are undefined or uneven. Mathematical Property: Supports ranking and comparison. We can determine if \(x_i > x_j\) or \(x_i < x_j\), but the difference \(x_i - x_j\) has no quantitative meaning. Permissible Operations: Median, Mode, Percentiles, Rank Correlation. Intuition: We know the order, but we don't know the distance between the values. Example: Likert scale (\(1=\text{Strongly Disagree}, 5=\text{Strongly Agree}\)), Letter Grades (\(A > B > C\)), Economic Status (Low, Middle, High).

docs.title: 3. Interval Scale
docs.text: Meaning: Numerical data where both the order and the exact differences (intervals) between values are meaningful, but there is no true (absolute) zero point. Mathematical Property: Supports addition and subtraction. The difference \(\Delta x = x_i - x_j\) is meaningful. However, ratios \(x_i / x_j\) are mathematically invalid because the zero point is arbitrary. Permissible Operations: Mean, Median, Mode, Standard Deviation, Addition, Subtraction. Intuition: Zero does not mean "nothing" or "absence of the quantity". Example: Temperature in Celsius (\(0^\circ\text{C}\) does not mean no temperature), Calendar Year (\(2000\) AD, \(2020\) AD).

docs.title: 4. Ratio Scale
docs.text: Meaning: Numerical data possessing all the properties of an interval scale, along with a true, non-arbitrary zero point indicating the complete absence of the quantity. Mathematical Property: Supports all arithmetic operations, including multiplication and division. The ratio \(r = x_i / x_j\) is highly meaningful. Permissible Operations: Mean, Median, Mode, Geometric Mean, Coefficient of Variation, all arithmetic operations. Intuition: Zero means literally zero (none). Therefore, statements like "twice as much" make perfect sense. Example: Height (\(180\text{ cm}\) is exactly twice as tall as \(90\text{ cm}\)), Weight, Income (\(\$0\) means no income), Distance, Age. [Source: Existing Notes]

docs.title: 7. Data Representation Formats: Ungrouped vs Grouped
docs.text: When dealing with large datasets, the way data is presented mathematically profoundly impacts how analysis is conducted.

docs.title: 1. Raw Ungrouped Data
docs.text:
Meaning: A simple list of individual numerical observations exactly as they were recorded. Formal definition: A set of observations \(X = \{x_1, x_2, \dots, x_N\}\) where each \(x_i\) is an individual raw data point. Example: The ages of 10 students:

\[ X = \{14, 17, 18, 18, 22, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32\} \]

Advantage: Retains 100% of the original information precision. Disadvantage: Very difficult to interpret or identify patterns when the dataset is large (\(N > 50\)).

docs.title: 2. Grouped Class Table (Frequency Distribution)
docs.text:
Meaning: Data that has been organized into non-overlapping continuous class intervals, with counts (frequencies) for how many raw data points fall into each interval. Components: - Class Interval \([a, b)\): The range of values defined by a lower limit \(a\) and upper limit \(b\). - Class Width (\(w\)): The difference between the upper and lower boundaries of a class.

\[ w = b - a \]
  • Midpoint (\(x_i\)): The central value of the class interval, used as the representative value for calculations (like the mean).
\[ x_i = \frac{a + b}{2} \]
  • Frequency (\(f_i\)): The number of observations falling into the \(i\)-th class interval.
  • Relative Frequency: The proportion of total observations falling into the class.
\[ \text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{f_i}{N} \]

where \(N = \sum f_i\) is the total number of observations. - Cumulative Frequency (\(CF\)): The running total of frequencies through the classes.

docs.title: Example: Creating a Grouped Data Table
docs.text:
Given: A dataset of \(N=10\) observations: \(X = \{14, 17, 18, 18, 22, 25, 26, 28, 30, 32\}\). We want to group this into intervals of width 10, starting from 10.

Step-by-step Solution: 1. Define Intervals: \([10, 20), [20, 30), [30, 40)\). 2. Count Frequencies (\(f_i\)): - \([10, 20)\): Values are 14, 17, 18, 18. Count = 4. - \([20, 30)\): Values are 22, 25, 26, 28. Count = 4. - \([30, 40)\): Values are 30, 32. Count = 2. 3. Calculate Midpoints (\(x_i\)): - For \([10, 20)\): \(x_1 = \frac{10+20}{2} = 15\). - For \([20, 30)\): \(x_2 = \frac{20+30}{2} = 25\). - For \([30, 40)\): \(x_3 = \frac{30+40}{2} = 35\). 4. Calculate Relative Frequencies: \(f_i / N\). 5. Calculate Cumulative Frequencies: Running sum.

Resulting Table:

Class Interval \([a, b)\) Midpoint (\(x_i\)) Frequency (\(f_i\)) Relative Frequency (\(f_i / N\)) Cumulative Frequency (\(CF\)) \(10 - 20\) \(15\) \(4\) \(0.40\) \(4\) \(20 - 30\) \(25\) \(4\) \(0.40\) \(8\) \(30 - 40\) \(35\) \(2\) \(0.20\) \(10\) Total — \(N = 10\) \(1.00\) — [Source: Existing Notes]

docs.title: 8. Types of Digital Data (Based on Structure)
docs.text:
Digital data is fundamentally categorized into three types based on how it is formatted and stored.

graph TD
    Data[Data]
    Data --> Struc[Structured]
    Data --> Semi[Semi-structured]
    Data --> Unstruc[Unstructured]

    Struc --> ERP[Enterprise Resource Planning, SQL]
    Semi --> Call[Logs, JSON, XML]
    Unstruc --> FB[Facebook, YouTube, Images]

docs.title: 1. Structured Data
docs.text: Meaning: Data that is highly organized, strictly adhering to a predefined data model or schema, usually formatted in rows and columns. Sources: Databases such as Oracle, DB2, Teradata, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Spreadsheets (MS Excel), OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) systems. Characteristics: - Organized in rows and columns. - Stored in relational databases. - Easily searchable using queries like SQL. Working with Structured Data (Advantages): - Easy Insert/Update/Delete operations. - High-performance Indexing and Searching. - Robust Transaction processing (ACID properties). - High Security and Scalability. Examples: Excel sheets, SQL tables, Baggage info, Employee schedules. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slides 6-8]

docs.title: 2. Semi-Structured Data
docs.text:
Meaning: Data that does not reside in a rigid relational database but contains organizational properties (tags, markers) that make it easier to analyze than raw unstructured text. Sources: XML (eXtensible Markup Language), Other Markup Languages, JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), Logs, Email metadata. Characteristics: - Inconsistent or flexible structure. - Self-describing using label/value pairs. - Schema information is often blended seamlessly with data values. - Data objects may have different attributes not known completely beforehand. Examples: JSON payloads, XML configuration files, Feedback forms, Inventory logs. Example snippet: 

{
  "ReceiptID": "12345",
  "Store": "Duty-Free",
  "PassengerID": "P002",
  "Items": [
    { "ItemName": "Perfume", "Price": "50 USD", "Quantity": 1 }
  ]
}
[Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slides 9-10, 22]

docs.title: 3. Unstructured Data
docs.text: Meaning: Data that has no predefined format, structure, or schema, making it difficult to collect, process, and analyze using conventional relational tools. Sources: Web pages, Images, Free-form text, Audios, Videos, Body of Emails, Text messages, Chat conversations, Social media data, Word documents. Characteristics: - Massive in volume (constitutes the vast majority of real-world data). - Hard to categorize mathematically. - Requires advanced techniques like Natural Language Processing (NLP), Data mining, Text analytics, and Noisy text analytics to extract value. Examples: Airport flight announcements (audio file), CCTV video recordings of passenger interactions, Tweets ("Stuck at the airport due to flight delay #frustrated"), handwritten notes. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slides 11-12, 21]

docs.title: Case Study 1: Busy Airport
docs.text: Imagine you are at a busy airport with passengers checking in, waiting in lounges, shopping, and interacting with staff. Different data types are generated: - Structured Data: - Flight Information Table: Contains Flight_Number, Departure_Time, Arrival_Time, Gate_Number, From, To (e.g., AI202, 18:30, Mumbai to Delhi, Gate 5). - Passenger Information Table: Contains Passenger ID, Name, Passport No, Flight No, SeatNo, BoardingTime (e.g., P001, Alice, M1234567, AI202, 12A, 18:15). - Semi-Structured Data: - Shopping Receipts: Electronic receipts from duty-free stores in XML/JSON format. - Check-in Data: Logs combining structured elements (timestamps) with unstructured errors in XML format. - Unstructured Data: - Announcements: Audio files of public address system ("Flight AB123 is now boarding"). - Passenger Interactions: Video files from security cameras. - Social Media Posts: Free-form text tweets about the travel experience. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slides 16-23]

docs.title: Case Study 2: City Shopping Mall
docs.text: At a mall, people are browsing, looking for discounts, filling feedback forms, and standing at billing counters. - Structured: Transaction records at the billing counter (Item ID, Quantity, Price, Total Amount). - Semi-Structured: Customer feedback forms stored as JSON files on an iPad. - Unstructured: Security CCTV footage monitoring browsing behavior, or free-form comments written on the back of a receipt. [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slide 25]

docs.title: Exercise: Place in the Basket
docs.text: Task: Categorize the following words. - Email: Unstructured (Body) / Semi-structured (Headers) - MS Access: Structured - Images: Unstructured - Database: Structured - Chat conversations: Unstructured - Relations/Tables: Structured - Facebook: Unstructured - Videos: Unstructured - MS Excel: Structured - XML: Semi-Structured Solution Matrix: - Structured: MS Access, Database, Relations/Tables, MS Excel - Unstructured: Email, Images, Chat conversations, Facebook, Videos - Semi-Structured: XML [Source: 2.Types of Data.pdf, Slides 13-14]

docs.text:

docs.title: 11. Edge Cases & Practical Pitfalls
docs.text:
Scenario / Edge Case Risk / Problem Correct Handling Numerical Labels for Categories Treating Zip Code (\(90210\)) or Patient ID (\(1004\)) as Ratio data simply because they are numbers. Treat strictly as Nominal. Calculating the mean zip code is mathematically invalid and meaningless. Arbitrary Zero Trap Computing ratios on Interval data. E.g., claiming \(20^\circ\text{C}\) is twice as hot as \(10^\circ\text{C}\). \(20^\circ\text{C}\) is not twice as hot because \(0^\circ\text{C}\) is not absolute zero. Convert to Kelvin (Ratio scale) if a ratio is required. Ordinal Non-Uniformity Calculating the mean on Likert ratings (\(1=\text{Poor}\) to \(5=\text{Excellent}\)). Interval distances between ratings are strictly unknown. Use Median or Mode for statistical reporting instead of Mean. Discrete Data behaving Continuous Dealing with extremely large countable discrete numbers (e.g., population \(1,234,567\) or website clicks). In large-scale modeling, it is often mathematically convenient to model these as continuous variables, even though they are technically discrete.

[Source: Existing Notes]

docs.title: 1. Nominal Category Equality
docs.text:
Determines if two labels are the same.

\[ x_i = x_j \quad \text{or} \quad x_i \neq x_j \]

docs.title: 2. Ordinal Rank Ordering
docs.text:
Determines the strict ordering between two elements.

\[ x_i > x_j \quad \text{or} \quad x_i < x_j \]

docs.title: 3. Interval Difference
docs.text:
Calculates the exact quantitative difference between two measurements.

\[ \Delta x = x_i - x_j \]

docs.title: 4. Ratio Proportion
docs.text:
Calculates the multiplicative relationship between two measurements.

\[ r = \frac{x_i}{x_j} \quad \text{where } (x_j \neq 0) \]

docs.title: 5. Grouped Data Class Width
docs.text:
Determines the size of each continuous interval in a frequency distribution.

\[ w = b - a \]

Where \(b\) is the upper boundary and \(a\) is the lower boundary.

docs.title: 6. Grouped Data Midpoint
docs.text:
Calculates the representative center value of an interval.

\[ x_i = \frac{a + b}{2} \]

docs.title: 7. Relative Frequency
docs.text:
Calculates the proportion of total observations falling into a specific interval.

\[ \text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{f_i}{N} \]

Where \(f_i\) is the class frequency and \(N = \sum f_i\) is the total number of observations.

docs.title: Definition Sheet
docs.text:
• Data: A collection of facts, numbers, words, observations or other useful information.
  • Data Mining: The process of discovering interesting patterns and knowledge from large amounts of data.
  • KDD: Knowledge Discovery in Databases, the complete process from data cleaning to knowledge presentation.
  • Primary Data: Data collected firsthand for a specific purpose (surveys, interviews).
  • Secondary Data: Data already collected and available (internet, books).
  • Qualitative Data: Categorical data representing attributes without numerical value.
  • Quantitative Data: Numerical data representing measurable quantities.
  • Discrete Data: Quantitative data taking on distinct, countable integer values.
  • Continuous Data: Quantitative data taking on any real numerical value over an interval.
  • Nominal Scale: Categorical data acting purely as labels with no inherent rank order.
  • Ordinal Scale: Categorical data with ordered ranks but mathematically undefined intervals between them.
  • Interval Scale: Numeric data with equal intervals between points but an arbitrary, non-absolute zero.
  • Ratio Scale: Numeric data with equal intervals and an absolute true zero point, permitting multiplication/division.
  • Structured Data: Highly organized tabular data strictly adhering to a predefined relational database schema.
  • Semi-Structured Data: Self-describing data with flexible tags (e.g., JSON, XML) lacking rigid tables.
  • Unstructured Data: Freeform data (text, video, audio) with no predefined schema, difficult to categorize.
  • Grouped Data: Observations organized into continuous non-overlapping class intervals to compress large datasets.

docs.title: Important Concepts
docs.text:
• The distinction between the 4 levels of measurement (Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio) is heavily tested.
  • Distinguishing between Structured, Semi-Structured, and Unstructured data based on examples.
  • The step-by-step process of KDD.

docs.title: Potential Questions & Answers
docs.text:
Q1: Why is temperature in Celsius classified as Interval scale rather than Ratio scale? A: Celsius has an arbitrary zero point (\(0^\circ\text{C}\) is merely the freezing point of water, not the total absolute absence of thermal energy). Consequently, ratios are invalid; \(40^\circ\text{C}\) is not twice as hot as \(20^\circ\text{C}\).

Q2: Differentiate between structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data with examples. A: Structured data has a fixed tabular schema organized into rows and columns (e.g., SQL customer table). Semi-structured data contains self-describing tags or markers without rigid tables (e.g., JSON payload, XML). Unstructured data lacks a schema completely and cannot be fit into tables (e.g., an MP4 CCTV video file or a free-text tweet).

Q3: Can the arithmetic mean be reliably calculated on ordinal data? Explain. A: Strictly speaking, no. Ordinal data lacks uniform, defined distances between its ranks (e.g., the exact quantitative difference between a "Satisfied" and "Neutral" rating is unknown and may not equal the difference between "Neutral" and "Dissatisfied"). Median and Mode are the only statistically valid measures of central tendency for ordinal data.

Q4: Outline the steps of the Knowledge Discovery in Databases (KDD) process. A: The KDD process consists of seven sequential steps: Data cleaning (removing noise), Data integration (combining sources), Data selection (retrieving relevant records), Data transformation (summarizing into mining formats), Data mining (applying algorithms), Pattern evaluation (identifying useful knowledge), and Knowledge presentation (visualization).

Q5: In an airport setting, classify the following into Structured, Semi-Structured, or Unstructured data: a Tweet complaining about a delay, a JSON file containing a duty-free receipt, and an SQL table of flight departure times. A: The SQL table is Structured. The JSON receipt is Semi-Structured. The Tweet is Unstructured.

Q6: What is the primary difference between discrete and continuous quantitative data? A: Discrete data can only take on specific, distinct countable values (e.g., number of children: 1, 2, 3), whereas continuous data can take on any real infinite fractional value within a range (e.g., exact weight: \(75.423\text{ kg}\)).

Q7: Calculate the class width, midpoint, and relative frequency for the interval \([20, 30)\) if its frequency is 4 and the total number of observations \(N\) is 10. A: Class Width \(w = 30 - 20 = 10\). Midpoint \(x = (20 + 30) / 2 = 25\). Relative Frequency = \(4 / 10 = 0.40\).

Q8: Explain the difference between primary and secondary data sources. A: Primary data sources are original data collected directly for a specific investigation (e.g., door-to-door surveys, personal interviews). Secondary data sources are pre-existing data compiled by others (e.g., Internet databases, books, newspapers).

docs.title: Ch 3 - Dataset & Attributes
docs.text: Course: Data Analysis and Visualization Primary Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf Files Integrated: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, ch3_text.txt

docs.title: 1. Chapter Overview
docs.text: This chapter covers datasets, attribute types, and structural properties in data mining. Key topics include attribute taxonomy (nominal, binary, ordinal, numeric), dataset structures (record, graph, ordered, time series), matrix representations (Data Matrix, Document-Term Matrix), characteristics (dimensionality, sparsity, resolution), and data representation formats. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 1]

docs.title: Definition: Attribute
docs.text: Meaning: An attribute is a data field representing a characteristic or feature of a data object. Synonyms: Feature (Machine learning), Variable (Statistics), Column (Databases), Dimension (Data warehousing). Example: Customer attributes: Customer ID, Name, Address. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 2]

docs.title: Definition: Attribute Vector and Distribution
docs.text: Meaning: An attribute vector is a set of attributes describing an object. Distribution types based on attribute count: - Univariate: Involves one attribute. - Bivariate: Involves two attributes. - Multivariate: Involves multiple attributes. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 3]

docs.title: 3. Qualitative vs Quantitative Data
docs.text:
graph TD
    Data[Types of Data Based on Nature]
    Data --> Qual[Qualitative Data]
    Data --> Quant[Quantitative Data]

    Qual --> Nom[Nominal]
    Qual --> Ord[Ordinal]

    Quant --> Disc[Discrete]
    Quant --> Cont[Continuous]

docs.title: Qualitative (Categorical) Data
docs.text: Information representing characteristics that you do not measure with numbers. Observations fall within a countable number of groups. It captures subjective information or things not easily measured. Examples: Taste, the color of a car, architectural style, marital status. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 31, 34]

docs.title: Quantitative (Numerical) Data
docs.text: Information recorded as numbers representing an objective measurement or a count. Examples: Age, height, temperature, weight, count of transactions. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 31, 37]

docs.title: 4. Attribute Taxonomy
docs.text:
graph TD
    Attr[Attribute Types]
    Attr --> Nom[Nominal: Unordered Categories]
    Attr --> Bin[Binary: Two States]
    Attr --> Ord[Ordinal: Ordered Categories]
    Attr --> Num[Numeric: Quantitative]

    Bin --> Sym[Symmetric: Equal Importance]
    Bin --> Asym[Asymmetric: Unequal Importance]

    Num --> Int[Interval-Scaled: No Absolute Zero]
    Num --> Rat[Ratio-Scaled: Absolute Zero]

docs.title: 1. Nominal Attributes
docs.text: Meaning: Categorical values with no meaningful order (also called enumerations). They can be coded with numbers, but arithmetic operations are meaningless. Example: - Hair Color: black, brown, blond, red - Marital Status: single, married, divorced - Occupation: teacher, farmer, etc. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 5, 35]

docs.title: 2. Binary Attributes
docs.text: Meaning: A special nominal type with only two states, typically represented as 0 (absent/false) and 1 (present/true). Example: - Smoker: 0 = No, 1 = Yes - Medical Test: 0 = Negative, 1 = Positive Types: - Symmetric: Both states equally important (e.g., gender). - Asymmetric: One state more important than the other (e.g., HIV test result). [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 6]

docs.title: 3. Ordinal Attributes
docs.text: Meaning: Ordered categories where the interval or distance between them is unknown. They are treated as categorical, but the numbers have mathematical meaning purely in their ordering. Example: - Size: Small \(<\) Medium \(<\) Large - Grades: A+ \(>\) A \(>\) B+ - Satisfaction Level: 0 = Very Dissatisfied, 1 = Dissatisfied, 2 = Neutral, 3 = Satisfied, 4 = Very Satisfied. - Restaurant Rating: Scale from 0 to 4 stars. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slide 7, 36]

docs.title: 4. Numeric Attributes
docs.text: Meaning: Quantitative measurable values represented in integer or real values. Types: - Interval-Scaled: Equal intervals, but no true zero-point. Arithmetic difference is meaningful, but ratios are not. - Example: Temperature in °C or °F, Calendar dates. 20°C is 5° more than 15°C, but 20°C is NOT twice as hot as 10°C. - Ratio-Scaled: Has a true zero-point. Can compute ratios, differences, mean, median, mode. - Example: Years of Experience, Weight, Height, Income. ₹100 is exactly 10 times ₹10. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slides 8-10]

docs.title: Discrete vs Continuous Attributes
docs.text:
• Discrete: Finite or countably infinite values. Cannot be meaningfully divided into smaller increments.
  • Example: Hair Color, Zip Code, Age (0-110), Smoker (0/1). A household can have 1 or 2 cars, but not 1.6 cars.
  • Continuous: Infinite real values, can take on almost any numeric value including fractional/decimal values. Usually stored as floating-point.
  • Example: Height, Weight, Temperature. The mean height in India is 5 feet 9 inches for men and 5 feet 4 inches for women. [Source: 3.Dataset and Attributes.pdf, Slides 11, 38-39]

docs.title: 5. Dataset Types & Matrix Formats
docs.text:
graph TD
    DS[Dataset Types]
    DS --> Rec[Record Data]
    DS --> Gr[Graph Data]
    DS --> OrdDS[Ordered Data]

    Rec --> Flat[Flat Files / Relational DB]
    Rec --> Trans[Transaction / Market Basket]
    Rec --> DM[Data Matrix]
    Rec --> DTM[Sparse / Document-Term Matrix]

    OrdDS --> Seq[Sequential Data]
    OrdDS --> Seqs[Sequence Data]
